segments.say: Lesson 10. Message Queues & Event Streaming. Async processing, Kafka versus RabbitMQ/S Q S, pub/sub, consumer groups, delivery guarantees and backpressure.

A message queue lets one part of a system drop off work ("send this email") and immediately move on, while other workers pick it up and do it in the background. Here is an analogy. A restaurant ticket rail: the waiter clips the order and goes back to customers; cooks take tickets at their own pace. A rush just makes the rail longer, and nothing is lost.

Why does this matter? Decoupling, absorbing traffic spikes and background jobs are in almost every design. A few key words. Producer / consumer: Who adds messages / who processes them. Topic / queue: The named channel holding messages. Async: The caller doesn't wait for the work to finish. Dead-letter queue: Where repeatedly failing messages go. Kafka / RabbitMQ / S Q S: Popular queue and streaming systems.

segments.sec: Watch: Sync vs async: why queues exist
segments.say: Workers process emails and invoices whenever they can. A down service just means messages wait and retry later. Nothing is lost and the user isn't blocked.
Decoupling with a queue. Without a queue, the order A P I calls email, inventory and analytics synchronously. That's slow, and if one is down the whole order fails.
With a queue: the A P I publishes an OrderPlaced event and returns immediately. The producer doesn't know or care who consumes.
Pub/sub: each downstream service consumes at its own pace. Add new consumers without touching the producer.
Traffic spike? The queue absorbs the burst (load leveling). Workers autoscale on queue depth. That's backpressure handled.
Email worker keeps failing on a bad message leads to retry with backoff, then move it to a dead-letter queue for inspection instead of blocking everything.
Result: loose coupling, resilience, smoothing of spikes. The trade-off is eventual consistency and more moving parts.

Kafka: partitions & consumer groups. A Kafka topic is split into partitions: append-only logs. Messages with the same key (for example order id) go to the same partition, so order is preserved per key.
A consumer group splits partitions among its members: each partition goes to one consumer. Each consumer tracks its offset (read position).
Messages stay after being read (retention: days or forever). A new service or a bug fix can replay history. RabbitMQ/S Q S delete on ack.
Max parallelism equals number of partitions. A 4th consumer on 3 partitions sits idle, so plan the partition count ahead.

Delivery guarantees. At-most-once: may lose messages, never duplicates. At-least-once: never loses, may duplicate. The common default. Make consumers idempotent (dedupe by message I D). Exactly-once: possible within Kafka transactions. End to end it's really "at-least-once plus idempotency".

Patterns. Work queue: competing consumers share tasks (image resizing). Pub/sub fan-out: each subscriber gets every event. Event sourcing: the log of events is the source of truth. Outbox pattern: write the D B row and an "outbox" event in one transaction; a relay publishes it. Avoids the "D B updated but event lost" problem. Saga: distributed transaction as a chain of events with compensating actions.

Say it in the interview. "I'd decouple the write path from slow side effects with a durable queue: Kafka if we need high throughput, per-key ordering and replay, or S Q S/RabbitMQ for simple task queues. Consumers are idempotent because delivery is at-least-once, failures go to a D L Q, workers autoscale on lag, and the outbox pattern keeps D B and events consistent.".

Let's compare. Model: distributed log (pull), broker with queues/exchanges (push), managed queue (pull). Retention: days leads to forever, replayable, until acked, up to 14 days, deleted on ack. Ordering: per partition, per queue (mostly), F I F O queues only. Throughput: millions/sec, tens of thousands/sec, high, managed. Best for: event streaming, analytics, logs, C D C, task queues, complex routing, simple decoupling on A W S.

A likely interview question: Kafka versus RabbitMQ? A strong answer: Kafka is a distributed, retained, replayable log with per-partition ordering and huge throughput, good for event streaming and C D C. RabbitMQ is a broker with flexible routing that deletes on ack, good for task queues and request routing.
That's it for Message Queues & Event Streaming. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
